note: Criticises one-shot assessments and absent corrective action, which is a fair description of what most audits currently deliver.
title: A systematic review of algorithm auditing processes to assess bias and risks in AI systems
journal: Journal of Infrastructure, Policy and Development
explain_beginner: The paper reviews recent research on how people check AI systems for bias and risk. It looked at 22 studies from technology, law, and social sciences. Audits often test models, inspect them, challenge them, or involve affected people, in areas such as medical forecasts, loan approvals, and hiring checks. The review finds current audits are usually too technical, ignore real-life experiences, do not explain whose values matter, happen only once, rarely include affected communities, and seldom lead to fixes. It suggests audits should become ongoing, inclusive, and connected to decisions. This matters because AI increasingly affects important life opportunities.
explain_business: For executives, this review warns that checking AI for bias and risk is often treated as a one-time technical exercise. The paper examined 22 studies across technology, law, and social sciences and found that audits frequently miss real-world context, do not make value trade-offs clear, exclude affected communities, and rarely lead to corrective action. In practice, leaders should not treat an audit report as proof that a system is fair or low-risk. They should fund ongoing, inclusive reviews tied to clear accountability and follow-up fixes. This informs decisions about AI governance, deployment in high-impact areas such as lending, hiring, and medical forecasting, and investment in continuous auditing capabilities.
explain_practitioner: The author performed a structured review of published research on methods for auditing bias and risk in opaque AI. The search covered technology, law, and social science sources and selected 22 recent applied studies. The reviewed work includes numeric comparisons, model checks, stress tests, and stakeholder involvement, with examples in medical forecasting, loan approvals, and hiring checks. The analysis reports recurring weaknesses: overly technical framing, unclear value choices, single-time assessments, little involvement from affected groups, and few corrective actions after audits. Promising directions include subsidiarity analysis, people-focused tools, and corrective coding. The main result is that auditing should become ongoing, whole-system, inclusive, and tied to governance actions.
